# Weighing evidence (base rates and Bayesian updating) (`bayesian_reasoning`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/ideas.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Scientific method & philosophical ideas (`ideas`)
- Deps: needs probability_statistics; helped by fallibilism_provisional_knowledge
- Core idea: How much a piece of evidence should move you depends on how much more likely it is if the claim is true than if it is false, and on how plausible the claim was before. If a disease affects 1 person in 1,000 and a sign appears in 99 % of the sick but also in 5 % of the healthy, then of 1,000 people about 1 sick and 50 healthy show the sign, so a person with the sign has only about a 2 % chance of being sick. Work it out with counted people rather than percentages and listeners follow easily. The same rule explains why a surprising claim needs strong evidence and why testimony for a miracle or a marvellous cure must be weighed against the frequency of error and deceit.
- Pitfalls:
  - Confusing the chance of the evidence given the claim with the chance of the claim given the evidence (the prosecutor's fallacy)
  - Ignoring the base rate and treating a 'reliable' sign or test as near-certain proof
  - Assigning probability zero or one to anything, after which no evidence can ever change the belief
  - Dressing up a guess as a calculation by inventing the input numbers
- History: greece: 2nd c. BC – Carneades grades impressions by plausibility, without numbers; europe: 1748 – Hume's argument on testimony for miracles; 1763 Bayes's essay published by Richard Price; 1774 Laplace states the general rule and applies it widely; global: 1940–1941 – Turing uses sequential weighing of evidence against Enigma; 1950s onwards Bayesian statistics revived
- Read:
  - Thomas Bayes, An Essay towards solving a Problem in the Doctrine of Chances (1763)
  - Sharon Bertsch McGrayne, The Theory That Would Not Die (2011)
  - Gerd Gigerenzer, Reckoning with Risk: Learning to Live with Uncertainty (2002)
